title: Intersoft Consulting, General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) full text
text:
## GDPR: the structure a startup GC must know cold

The GDPR governs processing of personal data of individuals in the EU. Even a US startup is in scope if it offers goods or services to, or monitors the behaviour of, people in the EU.

## Article 6: six lawful bases for processing
You may only process personal data if you have at least one of these bases: (1) consent, (2) performance of a contract, (3) compliance with a legal obligation, (4) protection of vital interests, (5) a task carried out in the public interest, and (6) legitimate interests. There is no default: pick and document your basis before you process. Consent must be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous, and it must be as easy to withdraw as to give.

## Article 5: seven principles
Processing must satisfy: lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation (collect for specified, explicit, legitimate purposes); data minimisation (only what is necessary); accuracy; storage limitation (do not keep data longer than needed); integrity and confidentiality (security); and accountability (you must be able to demonstrate compliance).

## Article 4: definitions
Personal data is any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person. Processing is any operation performed on personal data, including collection, storage, use, disclosure, and erasure.

## Data subject rights (Chapter 3)
Access (Article 15), rectification (Article 16), erasure or the right to be forgotten (Article 17), data portability (Article 20), and the right to object (Article 21). Requests generally must be answered without undue delay.

## Article 83: administrative fines, two tiers
Lower tier: up to 10 million EUR, or in the case of an undertaking, up to 2% of total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. Upper tier (for breaches of basic principles, consent conditions, and data subject rights): up to 20 million EUR, or up to 4% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. These caps are why data protection is a board-level risk, not a checkbox.

title: California Office of the Attorney General, California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA)
text:
## CCPA / CPRA: California consumer privacy

The CCPA, as amended by the CPRA, gives California residents rights over their personal information and imposes duties on covered businesses.

## Consumer rights
Right to know: request the categories and specific pieces of personal information a business collected, the sources, the purposes, and the categories of third parties it was shared with or sold to. Requests are free and limited to twice a year. Right to delete: request deletion, subject to exceptions such as completing a transaction, security, or legal retention. Right to opt-out of sale or sharing: direct a business to stop selling or sharing personal information, including via a global privacy control; a business must wait at least 12 months before asking the consumer to opt back in. Right to correct inaccurate personal information. Right to limit use of sensitive personal information to what is necessary to provide the service. Right to non-discrimination: a business cannot deny goods or services, charge a different price, or provide a different level or quality of service for exercising CCPA rights.

## Definitions
Personal information: information that identifies, relates to, or could reasonably be linked with a consumer or household, including name, email, purchase records, browsing history, geolocation, biometrics, and inferences that create a profile. Sensitive personal information: government identifiers, financial account credentials, precise geolocation, contents of mail, email, and texts, genetic and biometric data, health, sex life, and racial, ethnic, religious, or union membership data. Sale: transfer to a third party for value. Sharing: disclosure for cross-context behavioral advertising.

## Which businesses are covered
A for-profit business doing business in California that meets any one threshold: gross annual revenue over $25 million; buys, sells, or shares the personal information of 100,000 or more California residents or households; or derives 50% or more of annual revenue from selling California residents' personal information. Nonprofits and government agencies are generally exempt.

## Response duties
Respond within 45 calendar days, extendable by another 45 days (90 days total) with notice. Provide at least two methods to submit requests (an online-only business may offer email only). You cannot require account creation to make a request, and verification information may only be used to verify identity.

title: Y Combinator, The SAFE (Simple Agreement for Future Equity)
text:
## The SAFE: Simple Agreement for Future Equity

Y Combinator introduced the SAFE in late 2013 as a flexible, one-document security for early-stage fundraising, with few terms to negotiate so startups and investors can close quickly and cheaply. A SAFE is not debt: it has no interest rate, no maturity date, and no expiration, which removes the ongoing administrative burden of a convertible note. The investor pays now and converts into equity at a future priced financing.

## Pre-money vs post-money SAFE
The original 2013 SAFE was a pre-money instrument, designed when startups raised a small amount before a priced Series A and SAFE holders were treated as early investors in that future round. YC released the post-money SAFE in 2018. Under the post-money SAFE, safe holder ownership is measured after (post) all the safe money is accounted for, treating the safe round as its own financing rather than a bridge to Series A. The post-money model lets founders and investors calculate immediately and precisely how much ownership of the company has been sold, which makes dilution easier to track.

## The types (post-money, for US companies)
1. Valuation Cap, no Discount. 2. Discount, no Valuation Cap. 3. Uncapped, with a Most Favored Nation (MFN) provision (no cap and no discount).

## How the economics work
A valuation cap sets the maximum company valuation used to convert the SAFE into shares, protecting the early investor if the priced round values the company higher. A discount lets the SAFE convert at a percentage below the price paid by new round investors. When both are present, the investor typically gets whichever gives more shares. The primary negotiated term is usually the valuation cap alone, which is why SAFEs cut legal cost and time.

## Why it exists
The SAFE enables high-resolution fundraising: a startup can close with an investor as soon as both parties are ready to sign, without waiting to coordinate a full round or negotiate a full stock purchase agreement.

title: GitHub, Choose an Open Source License (license comparison)
text:
## Open source license obligations

Picking a license is a legal decision with downstream obligations. The core split is permissive vs copyleft.

## Permissive vs copyleft
Permissive licenses (MIT, Apache 2.0, BSD, Boost) let others reuse, modify, and redistribute, including in proprietary and commercial products, without a duty to release source. Copyleft licenses (GPLv3, LGPLv3, MPL 2.0, AGPLv3) require making the complete source code of licensed works and modifications available under the same license, which can force your own code open if you distribute a combined work. This is the reason engineering teams must vet dependencies before shipping.

## MIT License
Permissions: commercial use, distribution, modification, private use. Conditions: include the license and copyright notice. Limitations: no liability, no warranty. The most permissive common choice.

## Apache License 2.0
Permissions: commercial use, distribution, modification, patent use, private use. Conditions: include the license and copyright notice, and state changes. Limitations: no liability, no trademark use, no warranty. Apache adds an express patent grant, which MIT lacks.

## GNU GPLv3
Permissions: commercial use, distribution, modification, patent use, private use. Conditions: disclose source, include the license and copyright notice, use the same license (strong copyleft), and state changes. Limitations: no liability, no warranty. Distributing software that links GPL code generally requires releasing your source under GPL.

## GNU LGPLv3
Same as GPLv3 but the same-license condition applies at the library level, allowing linking from proprietary code under narrower conditions.

## Mozilla Public License 2.0
Weak copyleft: disclose source and keep the same license at the file level, so modified MPL files stay open but you can combine them with proprietary files. Includes a patent grant.

## Practical rule
Permissive licenses shift almost all risk to the user (no warranty, no liability). Copyleft licenses attach source-disclosure and same-license conditions that can be incompatible with a closed-source product, so the obligation, not just the permission, is what matters.

title: USPTO, Trademark, patent, or copyright
text:
## The three kinds of intellectual property

Founders routinely confuse these. Each protects a different thing, is granted differently, and is administered by a different office.

## Trademark
A word, phrase, design, or a combination that identifies your goods or services and distinguishes them from competitors. It protects brand identifiers such as business names, logos, and slogans used in commerce. Example given by the USPTO: Coca-Cola for soft drinks. A trademark prevents others from registering confusingly similar marks for related goods or services. Federal registration (the R in a circle symbol) provides nationwide rights and legal advantages beyond common-law use (which is signaled by TM). Administered by the USPTO.

## Patent
Protects technical inventions such as chemical compositions like pharmaceutical drugs, mechanical processes like complex machinery, or machine designs, when they are novel and industrially applicable. Example: a new type of hybrid engine. A patent prevents others from copying, manufacturing, or selling the patented invention without permission. Administered by the USPTO.

## Copyright
Protects artistic, literary, or intellectually created works, such as novels, music, movies, software code, photographs, and paintings, that are original and exist in tangible form. Example: song lyrics from Frozen. Copyright grants exclusive rights to reproduce, distribute, and display the work and to prevent unauthorized copying. Administered by the US Copyright Office at the Library of Congress, not the USPTO.

## Why the distinction matters for a startup
A product name is a trademark question; the codebase and content are copyright questions; a novel algorithm or device may be a patent question. Confusing them leads founders to protect the wrong asset or to claim protection they do not have.

title: U.S. Copyright Office, What is Copyright?
text:
## Copyright basics

Copyright is a form of protection for original works of authorship that are fixed in a tangible medium of expression. This covers paintings, photographs, musical works, sound recordings, computer programs, books, movies, and architectural works.

## Two requirements: originality and fixation
A work must be independently created by a human author with at least a minimal degree of creativity, and it must be fixed, meaning captured in a sufficiently permanent medium such that the work can be perceived, reproduced, or communicated for more than a short time.

## Idea vs expression
Copyright protects expression only. It does not protect ideas, procedures, methods, systems, processes, concepts, principles, or discoveries. This is why a competitor can build a product with the same idea, as long as they do not copy your specific code or content.

## Exclusive rights of the owner
US copyright law grants the owner the exclusive rights to reproduce the work in copies, prepare derivative works, distribute copies to the public, perform the work publicly, display the work publicly, and, for sound recordings, perform them publicly by digital audio transmission.

## Automatic protection, but register to enforce
Copyright exists automatically upon creation and fixation. Registration is not mandatory, but it offers significant legal advantages for enforcement (registration is generally a prerequisite to filing an infringement suit for US works and enables statutory damages).

## Relationship to other IP
Copyright differs from patents, which protect inventions, and from trademarks, which protect words, names, symbols, or devices used as a source identifier on goods and services. For a software startup, the code is protected by copyright the moment it is written, but ownership vests in the human author unless it is a work made for hire or has been assigned in writing.

title: IRS, Independent Contractor (Self-Employed) or Employee?
text:
## Worker classification: contractor vs employee

The IRS uses common law rules to determine worker status. You must examine the entire relationship and consider the extent of the right to direct and control the worker. Getting this wrong is one of the most expensive mistakes a startup can make.

## Three categories of control
1. Behavioral control: does the company control or have the right to control what the worker does and how the worker does the job? 2. Financial control: does the payer control the business aspects of the job, such as how the worker is paid, whether expenses are reimbursed, and who provides tools and supplies? 3. Type of relationship: are there written contracts or employee-type benefits such as pension, insurance, and vacation; is the relationship continuing; and is the work a key aspect of the business?

## No single deciding factor
There is no magic or set number of factors that makes the worker an employee or an independent contractor, and no one factor stands alone. Factors that are relevant in one situation may not be relevant in another. You weigh all the evidence together.

## Consequences of misclassification
If you classify an employee as an independent contractor and have no reasonable basis for doing so, you may be held liable for employment taxes for that worker under Internal Revenue Code section 3509.

## Relief and forms
A business with a reasonable basis for treating a worker as a contractor may be eligible for relief if it filed consistent federal information returns and did not treat similar positions as employees after 1977. Either the business or the worker may file Form SS-8 to ask the IRS to make an official determination; that determination can take at least six months. A misclassified worker can use Form 8919 to report the uncollected Social Security and Medicare taxes owed on their pay.

title: 16 CFR 255.1, FTC Endorsement Guides: General considerations
text:
## FTC endorsements: general considerations (16 CFR 255.1)

Endorsements must reflect the honest opinions, findings, beliefs, or experience of the endorser. They cannot convey any express or implied representation that would be deceptive if made directly by the advertiser.

## Bona fide user requirement
When an advertisement represents that the endorser uses the product, the endorser must have been a bona fide user of it at the time the endorsement was given, and the advertiser may continue to run the endorsement only so long as it has good reason to believe the endorser remains a bona fide user. Reasonableness of that belief turns on factors such as new information about the performance or effectiveness of the product, a material alteration in the product, and changes in the performance of competitors' products.

## Liability, on both sides
Advertisers are subject to liability for false or unsubstantiated statements made through endorsements, or for failing to disclose material connections. Endorsers may also be liable for their own statements, particularly for representations that the endorser knows or should know to be deceptive. This is the key point founders miss: paying an influencer does not move the legal risk off the company; the advertiser remains on the hook for the influencer's claims.

## Advertiser duties
To limit exposure, advertisers should give endorsers guidance on making truthful, substantiated claims and on disclosing connections, should monitor what endorsers say, and should take action sufficient to remedy non-compliance and prevent future non-compliance.

title: 16 CFR 255.2, FTC Endorsement Guides: Consumer endorsements
text:
## FTC consumer endorsements and testimonials (16 CFR 255.2)

An advertisement that uses a consumer endorsement about the performance of a central attribute of a product will likely be interpreted as representing that the endorser's experience is representative of what consumers will generally achieve. The advertiser must therefore have adequate substantiation for that representation. Consumer endorsements themselves are not competent and reliable scientific evidence.

## The results not typical safe harbor is gone
A disclaimer such as Results not typical, or These testimonials are based on the experiences of a few people, is no longer enough to avoid deception. Instead, if the endorser's experience is not what consumers will generally achieve, the advertiser must clearly and conspicuously disclose the generally expected performance in the depicted circumstances, using concrete language such as The average homeowner saves $35 per month, or Most users lose 8 pounds, or The typical weight loss is 15 pounds.

## No manipulating reviews
The rule also prohibits advertisers from suppressing, boosting, or misrepresenting consumer reviews, regardless of the platform, so that honest consumer opinion remains visible. Suppressing negative reviews or seeding positive ones is treated as deceptive.

## Practical takeaway
For a startup marketing team, testimonials that showcase a best-case customer must be paired with an honest disclosure of typical results, and the underlying claim still needs the same substantiation as if the company made it directly.

title: 16 CFR 255.5, FTC Endorsement Guides: Disclosure of material connections
text:
## FTC material connection disclosure (16 CFR 255.5)

When there is a connection between the endorser and the seller of the advertised product that might materially affect the weight or credibility of the endorsement, and that connection is not reasonably expected by the audience, the connection must be disclosed clearly and conspicuously. Material connections include a business, family, or employment relationship, monetary payment, free or discounted products, early access, or the mere possibility of future compensation.

## Illustrative examples from the rule
A drug company that funds research on its own product must disclose that funding, because consumers would not expect the advertiser subsidized the study. A film star endorsing a food product in a commercial need not disclose payment, because viewers already expect celebrities are paid for commercials. A tennis player who discusses laser vision correction surgery on a talk show must disclose being paid as a spokesperson, because consumers might not realize a celebrity discussing a medical procedure has been paid; the same disclosure is required for a social media post even if the only compensation was free or discounted surgery. A physician endorsing an anti-snoring product must disclose an ownership stake or a share of sales. Using paid actors as consumer endorsers without disclosure is deceptive, and reviews incentivized with free product or payment require a clear disclosure. Company employees who promote the product in online communities must disclose the employment relationship, and bloggers who earn affiliate commissions from product links must disclose that arrangement.

## Clear and conspicuous
The disclosure must be difficult to miss and easily understood. Placement matters: it should be where the audience is not likely to miss it, and it should not be buried in a string of hashtags or hidden behind a More link. The FTC has said that a lone tag like sponsored or ad, or a platform's built-in paid partnership tool, can be inadequate. The ultimate responsibility for disclosure rests with the influencer and the brand, not the platform.

title: FoodChain ID, Updated FTC guidance on claims in advertising (substantiation)
text:
## FTC advertising substantiation doctrine

Under the FTC Act, advertising must be truthful and non-deceptive, advertisers must have evidence to back up their claims, and ads cannot be unfair. The substantiation requirement is the one founders underestimate: you must have adequate support for an objective claim before you publish it, not after a regulator asks.

## Reasonable basis, before publication
Advertisers must substantiate claims before publication. The FTC evaluates the consumer's understanding of the ad, not the marketer's intent. A firm's failure to have a reasonable basis for objective claims is itself an unfair and deceptive practice.

## Competent and reliable scientific evidence
For health and safety claims, the standard is competent and reliable scientific evidence, which typically means well-designed human clinical trials and evidence accepted by experts in the field, with higher-risk claims requiring stronger proof. Anecdotes and consumer testimonials are not a substitute for this evidence.

## Express vs implied claims and net impression
Express claims are direct statements, for example boosts immunity. Implied claims are messages a reasonable consumer takes from context, visuals, or a product name. The FTC judges the net impression of the ad as a whole, including text, product name, images, and charts, not just isolated sentences.

## Disclaimers do not cure a deceptive message
If the core message of the ad is misleading, adding a disclaimer will not fix it. Testimonials and endorsements must reflect typical results or clearly disclose otherwise, must be backed by the same level of evidence as a direct claim, and, for expert endorsements, must come from someone with relevant qualifications. Note the division of labor: the FTC has primary responsibility for advertising, while the FDA oversees product labeling.

title: Cornell Legal Information Institute, Work Made for Hire
text:
## Work made for hire

Work made for hire is the exception to the default rule that copyright vests in the human author. If a work qualifies as made for hire, the employer or commissioning party is considered the author and owns all rights under copyright law.

## Two categories only
A work is made for hire only if it fits one of two categories. First, a work prepared by an employee within the scope of their employment. Second, a work specially ordered or commissioned that falls into one of nine enumerated categories and is the subject of a written agreement signed by both parties stating it is a work made for hire. The nine categories include a contribution to a collective work, a part of a motion picture or other audiovisual work, a translation, a supplementary work, a compilation, an instructional text, a test, answer material for a test, and an atlas.

## Why contractors are the trap
Independent contractors and freelancers do not automatically create works made for hire simply by being hired and paid. Ordinary software development, for example, does not fall within the nine commissioned categories. Courts also apply an instance and expense test in some circuits, asking whether the hiring party induced the creation of the work and had the right to direct and supervise it. If the work-made-for-hire test is not met and there is no written agreement, copyright ownership remains with the creator, and the company must obtain a separate written assignment. This is why every contractor agreement needs both a work-made-for-hire clause and a present-tense assignment as a backstop.

title: Promise Legal, Founder IP Assignment: What Investors Check at Diligence (anti-pattern)
text:
## Anti-pattern: the missing or mis-drafted IP assignment

Founders typically assume that work created for the company automatically belongs to the company. That is legally incorrect. Under 17 U.S.C. 201(a) copyright vests automatically in the human author, not the entity. Without a written assignment, the founder personally owns the code, and that gap surfaces at every fundraise and acquisition.

## Two words that change everything: hereby assign vs agree to assign
Hereby assign is an immediate, present-tense transfer of title. Agree to assign is only a future promise, so the founder keeps ownership until an actual transfer happens. In Stanford University v. Roche Molecular Systems the Supreme Court confirmed that agree to assign language can lose to a later hereby assign contract signed with a third party. If your PIIA only says agree to assign, the company may hold nothing more than a contractual promise, not the IP.

## What must be assigned
Pre-incorporation code, patent-eligible inventions, trade secrets and know-how, domain names, brand assets, and written materials such as whitepapers, pitch decks, and technical documentation all vest in the individual creator absent a written transfer.

## Three non-negotiable PIIA provisions
1. Present-tense assignment language (hereby assigns). 2. A prior inventions schedule listing pre-formation IP the founder keeps out. 3. State-law carve-outs acknowledging California Labor Code 2870 and similar statutes in Washington, Minnesota, Utah, and Illinois, which protect inventions an employee develops on their own time without company resources.

## Timing and consideration
Execute the assignment at formation, not at the raise. When a founder signs after already contributing work, courts may question whether there is sufficient consideration to support the assignment, and the founder gains leverage. A late fix also has limits: a party must hold legal title on the day an infringement complaint is filed, and that requirement cannot be satisfied retroactively.

## Prior employer claims
An old employer's invention agreement can reach your startup's technology if the work was done on employer equipment, during business hours, or if it relates to the employer's business. The relates-to trigger is the most dangerous. Missing assignments are common cleanup items at Series A and especially at M&A diligence; the cleanup is possible but expensive and can trigger escrow or legal-opinion conditions, or in some cases sink the deal.

title: Common Paper, Cloud Service Agreement (Standard Terms and structure), CC BY 4.0
text:
## How a SaaS contract is structured

A modern SaaS deal is layered, not one giant document. The Common Paper Cloud Service Agreement (a free, open standard under CC BY 4.0) uses three layers: Standard Terms posted online and incorporated by reference; a Cover Page that holds the business details (the Order Form) and the negotiated legal specifics (Key Terms) and is signed by both parties; and the Framework Terms, which are the Standard Terms plus Key Terms functioning as a master agreement that can govern one or many Order Forms. If the Order Form conflicts with the Framework Terms, the Order Form controls. This mirrors the classic MSA plus order form plus DPA pattern.

## Commercial terms
Subscriptions are commonly 12 months. Fees are usually non-refundable except where a termination right allows a prorated refund. Payment is typically invoice-based with NET-30, or automatic charges. Auto-renewal is the default unless a party gives notice (often 30 or more days before the period ends).

## The clauses that matter
Warranties: the provider warrants it will not materially reduce the general functionality of the service during the term; the customer warrants it has rights to the content it submits; all other warranties are disclaimed. Limitation of liability: a general cap, often 1x the fees paid or payable in the prior 12 months, with a higher supercap for sensitive claims like data breaches, exclusion of consequential damages, and certain unlimited or carved-out claims such as indemnification. Indemnification: the provider typically covers third-party IP infringement claims about the service, and the customer covers claims arising from its content or misuse; the indemnifying party controls the defense and the other party cooperates. Confidentiality: mutual, with a reasonable standard of care, surviving termination. IP ownership: the provider keeps all right, title, and interest in the product; the customer keeps all right, title, and interest in customer content; the provider may use aggregated, de-identified usage data.

## Data protection
Before submitting personal data governed by GDPR, the customer must enter into a data processing agreement (DPA) with the provider. Certain data (health information, financial account numbers, government IDs, GDPR special categories) is restricted unless authorized. Related agreements plug in as needed: a DPA for GDPR data, an SLA (included in a minority of deals), a professional services addendum, and a BAA for HIPAA-regulated health data.

## Term and termination
Termination for cause typically requires a 30-day cure period for a material breach, with immediate termination for an incurable breach. The provider may suspend for non-payment or misuse. Force majeure lets either party terminate if an unforeseeable event prevents material performance for 30 or more consecutive days.

title: Holloway, The Holloway Guide to Equity Compensation
text:
## Startup equity, vesting, 83(b), options, and the cap table

## Restricted stock and vesting
Restricted stock is direct company ownership subject to conditions: transfer restrictions and a vesting schedule enforced by a repurchase right that lapses over time as the person keeps working. The standard startup pattern is a 4-year vesting schedule with a 1-year cliff, which means nothing vests until the one-year mark, then the equity vests incrementally (often monthly) thereafter. Vesting protects the company and remaining founders if someone leaves early.

## The 83(b) election (the 30-day trap)
An 83(b) election lets a recipient of restricted stock elect to pay tax on the fair market value at grant, before the stock vests, rather than being taxed on the (usually higher) value as it vests. The deadline is strict and non-negotiable: the election must be filed with the IRS within 30 days of the grant or option exercise. The IRS will not extend it, and the consequences are irrevocable. Founders who miss this window can face large, avoidable tax bills as their stock appreciates and vests.

## Stock options: ISOs vs NSOs
ISOs (incentive stock options) are tax-advantaged but can trigger the Alternative Minimum Tax on exercise. NSOs (non-qualified options) are taxed as ordinary income on exercise but are simpler. The strike price is the fixed price to buy each share, set at fair market value on the grant date.

## 409A valuation
Companies set the fair market value (and therefore the strike price) using a 409A valuation, typically done annually. A 409A value is usually much lower than what investors pay for preferred stock, often only a third or less, which is what lets option strike prices be affordable for employees.

## Cap table fundamentals
Track outstanding shares (actually issued), fully diluted shares (including the option pool and convertibles), and each holder's percentage (their shares divided by the total). The option pool typically reserves 10 to 20% of shares for employees. Understanding fully diluted ownership, not just outstanding, is essential when reading dilution from a SAFE or a priced round.

title: Stripe Atlas, Incorporation: why a Delaware C corporation
text:
## Why venture-backed startups incorporate as a Delaware C corporation

## Delaware
Delaware has a long-established body of corporate law that has been tested in its courts over many years, giving a high degree of predictability in disputes. It is the only state with a separate business court, the Court of Chancery, staffed by judges who specialize in corporate matters and decide cases without juries. Investors are comfortable with Delaware because it is familiar; the large majority of venture-backed companies and US IPOs are Delaware corporations. Founders who form elsewhere or as another entity type are often asked by investors to convert to a Delaware C corporation as a condition of investment.

## C-corp vs LLC or S-corp
Venture investors overwhelmingly prefer the C corporation. LLCs are cheaper and simpler to run but are far less common among high-growth tech companies seeking venture funding, because their pass-through taxation and membership structure do not fit stock options, preferred stock, and institutional investors. An S corporation cannot have the multiple share classes and entity or foreign shareholders that venture financing requires.

## What to set up at formation
Beyond choosing the entity, founders establish the capitalization: the number of authorized shares, a low par value, founder stock issued and (usually) subject to vesting, and an option pool reserved for employees. Doing incorporation and founder stock correctly at the start, including the 83(b) election window and IP assignment, avoids expensive cleanup later.

## Practical note
Incorporating too early can create small ongoing costs and filings; incorporating too late can create tax and IP-ownership problems. The right moment is generally when you are ready to issue founder equity, take on money, or hire, because that is when clean stock, vesting, and assignments matter.

title: WilmerHale Launch, Deciphering a Preferred Stock Term Sheet
text:
## Reading a priced-round (preferred stock) term sheet

A priced round sells preferred stock to investors and is governed by a term sheet split into economic terms and control terms. A GC must know what each lever does.

## Economics
Valuation and price: the pre-money valuation drives the investor's purchase price and ownership percentage. Option pool: a larger option pool lowers the effective price because the pool typically dilutes existing holders, not the new investor (the option pool shuffle). Dividends: venture companies rarely pay dividends, but accruing dividends automatically accumulate on preferred like interest and are paid on a sale ahead of common.

## Liquidation preference
Preferred holders receive a specified amount before common on a sale or liquidation. Participating preferred investors recoup their investment first and then also share the remaining proceeds by ownership percentage (the double dip). Non-participating preferred holders choose between recouping their preference or converting to common and sharing pro rata, but not both, which is more founder-friendly and is the market norm.

## Anti-dilution
Preferred usually converts to common at a 1-for-1 ratio at first. If the company later sells shares below the original price (a down round), the conversion ratio adjusts upward for the preferred. Weighted-average anti-dilution uses a formula based on the new price and the number of new shares and is considered more equitable. Full ratchet resets the conversion price all the way to the new lower price and is far more punitive to founders and common holders.

## Control
Board composition: investors typically require at least one board seat, and lead investors in later rounds seek more. Protective provisions: separate approval of the preferred is required for material actions such as a sale, new financing, changes to the capital structure, affiliate transactions, or taking on debt. Preemptive (pro rata) rights let investors participate in future rounds to maintain their ownership percentage. Drag-along rights can compel common holders to vote for a sale approved by the preferred, potentially forcing a transaction the founders do not want.

title: CRV, Pro Rata Rights: A Founder's Guide to Term Sheets
text:
## Pro rata rights

Pro rata rights are contractual provisions that let existing investors participate in future financing rounds at a level that maintains their current ownership stake. For example, an investor who owns 10% can invest more in the Series A to preserve that 10% as new investors come in.

## The math
The pro rata amount is the investor's ownership percentage times the total size of the new round. An investor holding 8% of a company would need to invest $400,000 in a $5 million Series A to hold their 8%. Investors typically get a window, often around 20 days, to respond to a participation notice.

## Why investors want them
Pro rata rights are a portfolio-management tool that prevents the ownership an investor worked to secure in the seed round from shrinking with every new round. In breakout companies, early investors who exercised pro rata rights turned small initial checks into outsized returns by holding ownership as the valuation rose.

## Founder tradeoffs
Benefits: granting pro rata signals committed backers and can be valuable negotiating currency in a term sheet. Drawbacks: granting these rights broadly leads to cap-table overcrowding and constrained flexibility in later rounds. If too many existing investors exercise, there may be too little allocation left for a growth-stage lead that expects 15 to 20% ownership. Because the structure set early persists through later rounds, founders should be selective about who gets pro rata and how broadly it is written.
